newsitem.title: UK: Britain backs Poland's NATO membership bid.
newsitem.headline: Britain backs Poland's NATO membership bid.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Thursday threw Britain's weight behind a bid by Poland to join NATO in 1999.

Speaking to reporters after talks with visiting President Aleksander Kwasniewski, Major said it was very likely Poland would be one of the new members the defence alliance is planning to admit to mark its 50th anniversary in three years' time.

"I think Poland is a primary applicant for membership of NATO. I know that is very much the wish of the Polish government, and I think the British government see them as a future member as well," said Major, flanked by Kwasniewski.

He said there was no reason why Poland's membership of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation should be held up by a treaty that NATO is discussing with Russia, which has expressed concern about the alliance's planned eastward expanion.

"I don't think there's necessarily a correlation between the two -- one may happen before the other, it's difficult to tell," Major said, adding: "I don't think anyone has a veto on the expansion of NATO."
The prime minister also lent strong support to Poland's parallel bid to join the European Union. "The sooner that enlargement goes ahead the better," he said.
Earlier, Kwasniewski told the Royal Institute of International Affairs that Poland saw membership of NATO and the EU as historical opportunities not to be missed.

Kwasniewski, a former communist who replaced Solidarity leader Lech Walesa as president last November, argued that enlargement of NATO would strengthen the stability and security of the entire European continent, including Russia.
Noting that 82 percent of Poles supported NATO membership, he said Poland saw itself becoming one of the pillars of the alliance, not just an outpost.
"We are confident that Poland's accession to NATO will lead to a projection of stability and security into areas stretching beyond our Eastern frontier," he said.
Major's enthusiastic comments were the second boost for Poland's NATO aspirations this week.
On Tuesday, U.S. President Bill Clinton used a campaign speech to pledge that NATO would admit new members by 1999.

Kwasniewski, who also met opposition leaders and had lunch at Buckingham Palace with Queen Elizabeth, earlier welcomed a controversial vote by Poland's lower house house of parliament to relax laws on abortion.
"I will sign this law because it is a liberalisation of a very restrictive law that caused a lot of drama," Kwasniewski told Reuters. "I think we should be concentrating on sex education."
The new measure allows women to terminate their pregnancies before the 12th week if they face financial or personal problems, provided they undertake counselling.
